Baseline: 39 passing, 6 todo.

## Step 1: Naming Evaluation (First Priority)

The Green phase note says `requireDamagedItem`'s throw has moved from defensive to specified behaviour. Let me evaluate the naming across the module with that in mind.

**Names surveyed:**

| Name | Purpose | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| `requireInsurableType` | Throws if type not in price list | Fits — `require*` family, throw is the point |
| `requireInsuredItems` | Looks up policy items, throws on bad index | Fits |
| `requireDamagedItem` | Finds insured item for a damage, throws if uncovered | Fits — and now genuinely specified |
| `reimbursedAmount` | Pre-deductible reimbursable value | Fits |
| `damagePayout` | Reimbursement minus deductible | Fits |
| `capRemainingAfter` | Cap minus paid-so-far | Fits |
| `combinedRate` | Sum of applicable rates | Fits |
| `formsBlock` | Exactly 3 alike | Fits |

**Naming decision: keep all current names.** The `require*` trio is consistent, and each name states the fact it computes rather than the mechanism. The one thing the Green phase changed is not a name but a *doc comment*: `requireDamagedItem` documents the matching rule but says nothing about the throw now being specified behaviour, while its two sibling `require*` functions both explain why the throw is the interesting half.

## Step 2: APP Mass — `requireDamagedItem`

```
const requireDamagedItem = (insured: Item[], damage: Damage): Item => {
  const item = insured.find(({ type }) => type === damage.itemType);
  if (!item) throw new Error(`Policy does not cover an item of type ${damage.itemType}`);
  return item;
};
```

| Component | Count | Mass |
|---|---|---|
| Bindings (`insured`, `damage`, `item`, `type`, ×2 `damage.itemType`, `item`) | 7 | 7 |
| Invocations (`find`, `===`, `new Error`, template) | 4 | 8 |
| Conditionals (`if (!item)`) | 1 | 4 |
| **Total** | | **19** |

## Step 3: Simple Design Rules

**Rule 1 — Tests pass.** 39 green. Confirmed above.

**Rule 2 — Reveals intent.** One real gap, and it is the one the Green phase surfaced. `requireInsuredItems` and `requireInsurableType` each carry a "named for the rejection because the throw is the interesting half" note. `requireDamagedItem` has the same shape and now the same *status* — a test pins its throw — but its comment documents only the first-match rule. A reader comparing the three would conclude the third one's throw is still incidental.

**Rule 3 — No duplication.** I checked the `BASE_PREMIUMS`/`INSURANCE_VALUES` pair carefully. The existing comment is right and I will not touch it: `INSURANCE_VALUES[t] = BASE_PREMIUMS[t] * 10` holds for all six types today, but collapsing them would route premium modifiers into the cap, and the test at spec.ts:439 (cursed sword: premium 165, cap still 2000) is the executable guard. Coincidental agreement, not duplication. No other duplication found.

**Rule 4 — Fewest elements.** Considered inlining `formsBlock` and `capRemainingAfter` as single-expression helpers. Both name a domain fact ("exactly 3 alike is a block", "the cap belongs to the policy") that the call site would otherwise leave implicit. Keeping them.

## Step 4: Refactoring applied

The improvement is a Rule 2 one, on the doc comment.

content.text:
## Step 5: APP Mass After

Executable mass is **unchanged at 19** — the edit is entirely within a doc comment, so no constants, bindings, invocations, conditionals, loops, or assignments changed. Module-wide mass is also unchanged.

This is the Rule 2 / APP tradeoff working as intended: clarity improved at zero mass cost.

## Step 6: Decision Record

**Refactoring applied** (Rule 2 — Reveals Intent):

`requireDamagedItem`'s doc comment at `/home/experimenter/experiments/runs/2026-08-17_08-46-28_claim-office-example-mapping_v6.2-with-why-cleaned_opus-5-no-thinking/src/claim-office.ts:229` now records that its throw is specified behaviour, matching the convention its two `require*` siblings already follow.

Why this was the right target: the Green phase changed the *status* of that guard without changing a line of code. Before, all three `require*` functions had rejection-shaped names, but only two explained why. A reader comparing them would reasonably infer the third one's throw was still incidental — the sort of stale-by-omission comment that survives precisely because no code changed near it.

The comment also now flags the first-match consequence explicitly: two sword damage entries resolve against a one-sword policy. That is the exact tension the next-but-one test ("more damage entries of a type than the policy covers") will push on, and naming it marks the spot as unspecified rather than decided.

**Rejected, with reasons:**

- **Collapsing `INSURANCE_VALUES` into `BASE_PREMIUMS × 10` (Rule 3).** The 10× ratio holds for all six types, which makes this look like removable duplication. It is not. Modifiers apply to the base premium, so a derived table would let the 50% curse surcharge inflate the cap from 2000 to 3000 — paying more for insuring a cursed item. The test at `claim-office.spec.ts:439` is the guard. Two facts that agree numerically today, not one fact written twice.
- **Inlining `formsBlock` / `capRemainingAfter` (Rule 4).** Each is a one-line helper, so Rule 4 nominally favours removal, but each names a domain fact the call site would otherwise leave implicit. Rule 2 outranks Rule 4.
- **Renaming anything.** All eight names surveyed state the fact computed rather than the mechanism. No rename would improve intent.

## Report

```
Refactoring Complete
  Refactoring:  requireDamagedItem doc comment — records the throw as
                specified behaviour, aligning with its require* siblings;
                flags the first-match consequence as unspecified
  Mass Change:  19 → 19 (comment-only; Rule 2 gain at zero mass cost)
  Tests:        39 passing, 6 todo — all green
  Types:        npx tsc --noEmit clean
```

One note for the next Red phase, from reading the code cold: your prediction that "rejects a claim whose damage references an unknown item type" will be caught by the not-covered guard rather than an `INSURANCE_VALUES` check looks right — `requireDamagedItem` searches the policy's items, and an unknown type cannot be among them, so the throw fires for the same reason a known-but-uncovered type does. Worth deciding whether one guard serving both cases is the behaviour you want, or whether the MHPCO should distinguish "we don't insure that" from "your policy doesn't cover that" — the error messages differ in kind, and only the first is a price-list fact.
